rv.q: They — especially Peters — have transformed the entire show.
In its second incarnation, this revival has become a must-see for fans of either Sondheim or these wonderful actresses, a category which hopefully includes anyone who loves musicals.

What a difference a diva makes. Bernadette Peters steps into the six-month-old revival of 'A Little Night Music' with a transfixing performance, playing it as if she realizes her character's onstage billing -- 'the one and only Desiree Armfeldt' -- is cliched hyperbole.
This uneven but welcome revival of Sondheim's classic musical features a triumphant Broadway debut by Catherine Zeta-Jones.

In this version, Sondheim’s brilliant score is more effective in the quieter numbers than in such normally show-stopping set pieces as the first-act closer “A Weekend in the Country,” which here fails to have the desired impact.
But her acting, particularly in the first act, seems overdone, too strenuously self-aware.
Peter Marks called the production 'an unbalanced affair' and wrote that 'it's an unfortunate truth that Catherine Zeta-Jones is not ideally cast.'

But the behavior of the characters who wander through a twilight labyrinth of passion in early-20th-century Sweden has the exaggerated gusto of second-tier boulevard farce, of people trying a little too hard for worldliness.
Much as I esteem both women, neither one of them is well cast.
So as with much in this unbalanced affair, you find yourself wishing someone would send in something, anything.

Sondheim being Sondheim, you know that anything he writes is going to be intelligent, sophisticated, witty and lyrical, often self-consciously so. That's all there in the revival of his 1973 musical 'A Little Night Music,' directed by Trevor Nunn whose acclaimed London production made the trip across the pond.
It is more than serendipitous when the newcomers surpass their predecessors.
A certain balance has been restored to A Little Night Music in its current incarnation.
Peters simply soars with her heart-exposing version that shimmers with vulnerability.
As one exits A Little Night Music, the proper thing to do is sing Sondheim’s praises.
They are, without question, the two best reasons to see this revival.
If her glamorous presence is not exactly a perfect fit, she generates enough star power in the Trevor Nunn production to pack the houses in spite of the evening's shortcomings.

It's still possible to have a good time, because - much like their characters - Zeta-Jones and Lansbury pierce right through the nonsense of the reinterpretation to find the heart of fizzy intoxication still beating at this show's center.
They are, in a word, bewitching.

cn.t: This revival of Sondheim's waltz-infused classic receives mixed reviews, with critics praising the sophisticated score but divided on the production's execution. Bernadette Peters' later casting earns widespread acclaim for transforming the show.
